## Your first sheet

Every cell has a name: the column, then the row. The one in the top-left corner is called `A1`.

This sheet holds the revenue ({p0}) and the costs ({p1}) of a small company.
You don't need any more finance than that for this level.

A **formula** always starts with `=`. If you type `10+5` Excel reads text; if you type
`=10+5` Excel calculates. That's the whole difference.

But a spreadsheet doesn't exist to add numbers: it exists because a formula
points to **another cell**, and when that cell changes the result updates by itself.
In the last task you will point to a cell that is itself a formula. That's how a
model is built: in layers, not by rewriting everything each time.

M0A-02-OPERATORI.4:
## The order in which Excel calculates

A formula is not read left to right like a sentence: Excel follows the
**precedence** rules of maths. Multiplication and division happen before
addition and subtraction, always — even when they are written later in the formula.

If you type `=2+3*4` the result is {p0}, not {p1}: first
`3*4`, then `2` is added. To get {p2} you would need parentheses: `=(2+3)*4`.
Parentheses don't decorate a formula: they tell Excel which piece to calculate first.

### The scenario

A small business making custom gadgets. Each unit costs
{p3} to produce, {p4} came off the line this month, and there are
{p5} of fixed monthly costs (rent, utilities) regardless of how much is produced.

The first task is the simple case: **cost per unit × quantity, plus the fixed cost**.
Written exactly as it is described in words, the formula is already right — multiplication
beats addition on its own, no parentheses needed.

This month's revenue is {p6}. The online sales platform keeps a
commission of {p7} on the margin left after covering the fixed monthly cost.
The net margin is:

`= (Revenue − FixedCost) × (1 − Commission)`

Here the parentheses really matter. Look at what happens without them: if you typed
`=Revenue-FixedCost*1-Commission`, Excel would first compute `FixedCost*1` (which changes
nothing) and then subtract both that and the commission from Revenue, one after the other —
as if the commission, which is a fraction ({p8}), were a whole euro amount to be
taken off. The result would be {p9}, far from the
real margin of {p10}. The mistake is not a rounding issue: it's
multiplying the wrong thing by the wrong thing.

M0A-02-OPERATORI.14: Do (B7-B4) in parentheses first, then multiply everything by (1-B9), also in parentheses. Two groups, two pairs of parentheses.

## SUM doesn't work alone

Below are the expenses for {mese}, one row per line. That's eight cells, but not all
of them hold a number: someone in the office hasn't entered every amount yet.

**{RANGE}** is the range you'll work on for the whole level. The first four
requests are the family you already know by name: `SUM` for the total, `AVERAGE` for
the average, `MIN` and `MAX` for the extremes. All four, on their own, ignore anything that
isn't a number: you don't need to tell them, that's how they're built.

The last two look the same and aren't. `COUNT` counts **only
numbers**. `COUNTA` counts **everything that isn't empty**, numbers and text alike. In the
table below one line has no amount — an empty cell — and another has
only a handwritten note, not a figure. One is COUNT's exception, the other
COUNTA's: if the two formulas give you the same number, one of them is
wrong.

M0A-04-TIPIDATO.13:
## Not every number is a number

A cell can hold four different things: a number, text, a date
(which is a number in disguise) or a boolean (TRUE/FALSE). The blue below only tells you
that someone typed it by hand: it does **not** tell you the type. For that you need another
clue, free and always on — the **default alignment**. Numbers (and dates,
which are numbers) lean right. Text leans left. Booleans
sit in the middle.

The customer with code `{codiceClienteVisibile}` ordered a {p1} kg parcel
on {dataText}. Delivered: {p3}.

The customer code is made only of digits, yet it is text: if someone had
typed it as a number, the leading zero would have disappeared. That's the real reason — not a
whim — why codes with a leading zero are always written as text.

In the items table further down, the same thing happens to a quantity,
but for a different reason: it arrived already forced to text, the way an ERP
exports every column as text so as not to lose leading zeros elsewhere.
When you add it up with SUM, that cell will vanish from the total without any error,
any warning. Excel never complains about a number that is really text: it
just skips it. Keeping that in mind will save you hours later on.

M0A-05-ANCORAGGI.7:
## Why the `$` sign exists

When you copy a formula, Excel **moves the references along with it**. If in C7 you write
`=C2*B7` and copy it to D7, it becomes `=D2*C7`: everything slid one column. Almost always
that's what you want. Sometimes it's a disaster.

Here the base sits in **a single cell** (C2) and is {p0}. Inflation is {p1},
and the year multipliers that follow from it are already in row 6. The scenario
factors are in column B.

You need **a single formula** that fills all twelve cells. Which means that
inside that formula there are three references that must behave in three different ways:

- the base must never move
- the scenario factor must move down with the rows but not slide right
- the year multiplier must slide right but not move down

`$` locks: `$C$2` locks everything, `C$2` only the row, `$C2` only the column.
**F4 while editing cycles through the four forms.** Learn it now: you'll use it ten thousand times.

Watch the bottom-right corner: that's where a wrong anchor shows.
In the middle of the table it often produces a plausible number, which is why
this mistake survives all the way to the meeting.

M0A-06-DATE.2: In B4 compute the contract's expiry date: start from the start date in B2 and add the duration in days from B3. A date in Excel is just a number: you add it like any two numbers.

M0A-06-DATE.4:
## A date is just a number

Excel has no special "date" type: it counts days from a fixed epoch.
**1 January 1900 is day 1**. 2 January 1900 is day 2. And so on, one
more integer for every day that passes. When a cell "looks like" a date, underneath there is
always one of these numbers: the `dd/mm/yyyy` format is just the clothing Excel draws
it in, it doesn't change what's inside the cell.

Here a contract starts on **{p0}** and lasts
**{durataGiorni} days**. Since the date is a number and so is the duration, the expiry is
simply their **sum** — no function needed, just the `+` sign.

Below, a second case: a supplier was due to deliver by
**{p2}**, but only delivered on
**{p3}**. Here the operation is the opposite:
subtracting the older date from the more recent one doesn't give you a date, it gives you the
**number of days** between them. Adding moves forward in the calendar; subtracting two dates
measures it.
M0A-06-DATE.12: In B4 write `=B2+B3`: the start date plus the duration in days.
M0A-06-DATE.13: In B8 write `=B7-B6`: the more recent date minus the older one.

M0A-07-PERCENTUALI.6:
## The 1500% trap

A cell in percentage format doesn't hold "per cent": it holds a number, and
**multiplies it by a hundred when it draws it on screen**. Inside there's 0.15, on screen you see 15%.

Excel helps you in two cases:

- if you type `15%` **with the sign**, it stores 0.15 and applies the percentage format on its own;
- if the cell is **already** a percentage and you type `15`, it understands 15%.

The trap springs when the format comes **after**: you type `15` in a normal cell, then press
Ctrl+Shift+5, and the cell shows **1500%**, because it really holds 15. It's a mistake you
see immediately, which is why almost everyone makes it once and never again.

The board has set an EBITDA margin target of **{p0}** for next year.
B2 is a normal cell with no format: if you type "{p1}" and then format it,
you'll see {trappolaEsempio}.

## When the percentage comes from a formula

There's a second way, much more common in real models, for a percentage to end up in a
cell: not typed by hand, but **calculated as the ratio of two other cells**. The quarter
just closed had {p3} of revenue and {p4} of operating profit. The achieved
margin is that ratio — and since Excel does it, the 1500% trap can't
happen here: the division already produces the right fraction.

M0A-07-PERCENTUALI.13: No mental maths needed: in B7 type =B6/B5 and let the format do the rest.

M0A-08-FORMATI.8:
## The number doesn't change, its clothes do

A cell can really hold the number `0.18` and show `18%` on the surface, or
hold `8300000` and show `8,300,000.00 €`. The stored value isn't touched: it's the
**format** — a separate label attached to the cell — that decides how you read it. The
same number, three different outfits: that's why two cells that look different
can add up without surprises, and two cells that look the same can hide two
different values.

Below is the revenue of a company in the {sector} sector, split into Italy
({p1}) and international ({p2}). The total must be written
as currency.

EBITDA ({p3}) divided by revenue ({p4}) gives a margin that Excel
stores as {p5} and that the percentage format shows as {p6}.
If you leave it unformatted you'll read zero-point-something, and on a call that's where
you lose one second too many.

Finally two warehouse lots, {p7} and {p8} units: add them up, and
on a four-digit total the thousands separator makes the difference between reading it and counting it.

Three shortcuts to learn now, not to hunt for in the Home menu every time:

- **Ctrl+Shift+1** — number with two decimals and thousands separator
- **Ctrl+Shift+4** — currency
- **Ctrl+Shift+5** — percentage
